challenges.name: refresh-rotation-quiz
challenges.title: Sliding expiry, absolute expiry and what rotation alone buys
challenges.description: The refresh store of one CodeDev learner after a month of daily use, and an API log from a stolen-token investigation. Decide whether each statement is True or False.

questions.question:
The CodeDev refresh service uses these settings:

const REFRESH_TTL = 2_592_000;     // each refresh token: 30 days
const FAMILY_MAX_AGE = 7_776_000;  // a family: 90 days after login
// new record: expiresAt = Math.min(at + REFRESH_TTL, loginAt + FAMILY_MAX_AGE)

Learner 1042 logged in on her laptop at t = 1790000000 (family fam-81) and the web app has refreshed once a day since. Her latest record, written 30 days after login:

{ id: "r-412", familyId: "fam-81", status: "active", createdAt: 1792592000, expiresAt: 1795184000 }

Statement: "As long as the web app keeps refreshing at least once a month, learner 1042 will never be asked to sign in again on this laptop, because every refresh moves expiresAt 30 days forward."
questions.explanation: False. Each refresh slides the token expiry 30 days forward, but only up to the family's absolute limit: loginAt + FAMILY_MAX_AGE = 1790000000 + 7776000 = 1797776000. Records created after day 60 get expiresAt = 1797776000, and the first refresh at or after that second fails with token_expired, so she signs in again 90 days after login however often the app refreshes. That cap is deliberate: a token family copied by malware or left on a shared computer cannot live forever just by being used. The misconception is that sliding expiry alone bounds a session; it only bounds idle time.

questions.question:
The refresh service rotates by family but has no reuse detection yet: a rotated token is simply refused with token_rotated. Learner 1042's refresh cookie was copied by a malicious browser extension. API log:

09:00:00 POST /v1/auth/refresh ip=203.0.113.50  token=r-7 (fam-81)  -> 200 new token r-8, r-7 rotated
09:12:40 POST /v1/auth/refresh ip=198.51.100.7  token=r-7 (fam-81)  -> 401 token_rotated
09:15:00 POST /v1/auth/refresh ip=203.0.113.50  token=r-8 (fam-81)  -> 200 new token r-9, r-8 rotated

198.51.100.7 is learner 1042's home network; 203.0.113.50 is unknown to her.

Statement: "After the 09:12:40 request, the attacker still holds a working session: r-8 was accepted and rotated into r-9, while the learner's own browser is the one that was locked out."
questions.explanation: True. The attacker refreshed first with the stolen r-7, so the attacker received r-8 and the learner's browser was left holding the rotated r-7. Rotation alone then works against the victim: her refresh is refused, the attacker's chain continues (r-8, then r-9), and nothing in the system treats the refused r-7 as a sign of theft. Rotation limits how long a single stolen token is useful only when somebody notices the second use; that is reuse detection, the subject of lesson 8. The misconception is that rotating tokens is enough on its own to cut off a thief.

challenges.name: rotate-refresh-tokens-by-family
challenges.title: Rotate refresh tokens by family
challenges.description:
Build the refresh session service of the CodeDev API (POST /v1/auth/refresh) as a class RefreshSessionService. The test runner creates it with a list newTokens (the plaintext refresh tokens to hand out, in order), plays a script of operations at fake clock times (unix seconds) and prints { results, store }.

login(userId, deviceId, at): start a new family (ids "fam-1", "fam-2", ... in creation order across the whole service; every login starts a new family, even for the same user and device) and issue its first refresh token.

Issuing a refresh token (login and refresh): take the next unused string from newTokens; add a record { id, familyId, userId, deviceId, tokenHash, status: "active", createdAt: at, expiresAt } with id "r-1", "r-2", ... in creation order, tokenHash = sha256 hex of the plaintext (node:crypto createHash), and expiresAt = min(at + 2592000, familyLoginAt + 7776000): 30 days sliding, but never later than 90 days after the login that started the family. Also issue an access token with id "at-1", "at-2", ... expiring at at + 900 (not capped). Return { familyId, refreshToken, refreshExpiresAt, accessTokenId, accessExpiresAt }. Only successful operations consume a token, a record id or an access id.

refresh(token, at): find the record whose tokenHash matches the sha256 of token, then check in this order and throw new AuthError(code): no record -> "unknown_token"; status "revoked" -> "token_revoked"; status "rotated" -> "token_rotated"; at >= expiresAt -> "token_expired". A failed refresh changes nothing. Otherwise issue a new token in the SAME family, set the old record's status to "rotated" and its replacedBy to the new record's id, and return the new tokens. Do not revoke anything when a rotated token is presented (that is lesson 8).

logout(token, at): the same checks and errors as refresh; on success set that record's status to "revoked" (the runner prints { loggedOut: true }).

snapshot(): every record in creation order, with the fields above and replacedBy only on rotated records. Never store the plaintext token.
hints: Which pieces of state must survive between two operations of the script: per record, per family and per service? And which of them may change when an operation fails?

Write one private validate(token, at) used by both refresh and logout (hash, look up, then the four checks in the given order), and one private issue(...) used by both login and refresh. The 90-day limit belongs to the family, so remember each family's login time; a new record's expiresAt is the smaller of the two limits.

A similar chain on a different domain: a library card can be renewed, each renewal valid 14 days, but never beyond 60 days after the card was first issued on day 0. Renewing on day 10 gives a card valid until day 24; renewing on day 50 gives min(64, 60) = day 60; trying to renew on day 60 fails because day 60 >= 60. The old card is marked replaced and points to the new card number, and both stay in the ledger.

tests.name: Login then two refreshes: one family, old tokens rotated and linked by replacedBy
A rotated or unknown token is refused, no token is consumed, the current token still works
Sliding expiry: 1 s before expiresAt works, at expiresAt fails, failures consume no ids
Absolute cap: refresh expiry is clamped to login + 90 days, then the family ends
Two devices and two users: each rotation stays inside its own family
Logout revokes the presented token; revoked wins over expired; other device unaffected
Twenty refreshes every 15 minutes: exactly one active record, the first token is rotated
